title: I am 5 weeks into my first vibe-coding project, of course it's a game, learning+teaching at the same time is wild, and a lot of my friends are mad at me but I've been unemployed from a 30-year career in Software Development for so long I needed to do something with AI bcuz everyone else has moved on
author: LAGameStudio
selftext:
I would love to hear feedback not only on the image but on how people talk to their agents and what they're using and why and how.... I don't pay anything for the agent I'm using and that has been very helpful.  #notsponsored by the way, but I do mention it here for context.

Background:

I don't consider vibe coding to be the same skill as developing a game by hand, but I cannot deny the complexity and frustration it has generated.

During the first week, it went from 0->60 and I was amazed at the progress.  I have never successfully vibe coded anything I liked before.  The prompt?  "Let's create a game that is a hybrid of a 4X game and a RPG in the style of Starflight and Masters of Orion" ... the kind of game that defined my 1980s childhood and has influenced every game I've worked on since.

During the second week I was amazed at how I could add detail, and learned how to be very specific with the agent.  Things were slower.  What took 20 minutes before rarely was completing under 1 hour.  This is also the week I fed it a very long prompt and it actually implemented some of it, but then I learned I needed to read the thinking very closely. I had it make a very odd Design Lab voxel editor, but since then I've not used it.  Having worked on a similar game years ago entirely based on an editor, I knew not to go too far down this path.  I wanted something more like a "roguelike in space" reminiscent of Prospector; for some reason based on the games I picked it was shaping up to be just that... and I got it to implement and then ruin controller input...then fix it.

During the third week, I spent the entire week arguing with it over how to draw a better asteroid.  I shared photos, and explained graphics techniques to the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash agent about 10 times.  This is also when things started shifting with the Freebuff tool I'm using... lots of instability was coming.  Most of that is sorted now, but it was frustrating.  I also learned about [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md) and wrote one for the first time.  Definitely made things more reliable but also slower.  A single request can take me 2-3 hours now, when at the beginning it was done in minutes, not hours.

To date I have only provided 1 graphic, which is the title logo.  It has drawn everything using lines, polygons and shaders. Underlying Haxe is both UWP and Javascript. Everything is procedural, though that often means "variations on a few themes" .. attempts to expand this were not met with resistance, but it has been challenging to explain what I want, what should be different, and have the agent interpret that.  The context has grown and grown and I'm about to break off into a new chat forgetting the last month I think... this is because it is taking longer and longer.

A few days ago it implemented conversations with alien civilizations for the first time but they didn't really do much. I asked it to give it another go with some minor feedback, and it really impressed me today in that it is just that one iota closer to what I want and I can see a future.  Every new feature seems to need multiple passes before it resembles what I want, so I accept that it's not really able to make games like I would without my help, and that's a good thing.  I find myself writing more and more specifications and I wonder what a new project would look like now that I understand how to talk to it better...

But, it is really frustrating at the same time because it is slower and slower and is not 100% satisfying for various reasons...

Tech stack:

* Haxe / Heaps
* DeepSeek
* Freebuff

comments.author: gfe_TheHouse
comments.body:
I use codex, but this advice applies to Claude as well. I'm building in Godot. AI uses Obsidian to document everything.

 Eventually, and quickly, your game reaches a point where it's too big to put everything into context so folds into itself and makes a black hole for tokens where no amount of arguing will fix it. My agent MD has been instructed to always document in obsidian after almost every task. This reduces the context needed considerably. It's important to make every note atomic as well as link to parents and children. 

I also make sure to tell it why I'm doing something as often as I can, and it documents that. It will track intent and it will compare outcomes to your original intent if you're setup correctly. 

My agent is also responsible for inherently building test harnesses so that it knows to run the tests after each change. I can't understate how beneficial this step is. 

Using AI for art is tricky to get consistent. Good luck. 

I have found that I can send reference images for vfx, or shaders I've seen online, and it will do much better with examples. I haven't worked with 3d so I can't comment on that workflow.

replies.author: LAGameStudio
replies.body:
Can you elaborate on what Obsidian is?   There are multiple applications, projects and related products.  

I am working entirely on a local repo, will "Obsidian" run locally or is it a cloud service?

replies.author: gfe_TheHouse
replies.body: It's a glorified note taking app built on markdown files. It's local.

replies.author: gfe_TheHouse
replies.body: You should probably write or find an obsidian skill that just makes the notes consistent.

replies.author: LAGameStudio
replies.body: There is no skill but I use an mcp local server and I wrote a line in [Agents.md](http://Agents.md)

comments.author: ParalysisPRIME
comments.body:
Thirty years in and still willing to throw yourself at a new way of working is a good thing, whatever your friends say. What helped me most with agents on a growing codebase is close to what gfe_TheHouse said about notes: the agent forgets everything between sessions, so it needs somewhere outside the chat that holds the plan. I keep AGENTS.md short (conventions, how to run the build, where things live) and put the actual work elsewhere as small tasks with a clear done line. Each session then starts with "pick up task X, read the linked notes, update the task when you finish", which keeps the context small and stops it re-deciding things you settled back in week two

The other habit is asking it to write down why it made a choice whenever it touches something structural, like your Design Lab, so you can audit it later without re-reading the whole thinking log.

For the task side I use my own board, Brainloot (brainloot.io). It has an optional MCP server so the agent can read and update tasks on the board, which suits exactly this loop, and it never touches your code through it. The board runs on phone and desktop too, and if you ever move into Unity or Unreal the tasks can pin to objects in the editor. Starflight meets Master of Orion is a great pick, by the way.
